lessonInput.title: Conditionals and boolean logic
lessonInput.objectives: Use only the supplied claims to make a defensible distinction without adding outside facts.
lessonInput.topics: Claim 0: A conditional statement chooses which block of code to run based on whether a condition is true; if-else takes exactly one branch, and boolean operators (and, or, not) build compound conditions. Claim 1: An if statement runs its body only when the condition is true, and skips it when the condition is false. Claim 2: An else clause holds statements that run when the if condition is false. Claim 3: and returns True only if both conditions are true; or returns True if either is true; not inverts a single condition.
lessonInput.readings: OpenStax Introduction to Python Programming, §4.2 If-else statements; §4.3 Boolean operations

claims: A conditional statement chooses which block of code to run based on whether a condition is true; if-else takes exactly one branch, and boolean operators (and, or, not) build compound conditions.
An if statement runs its body only when the condition is true, and skips it when the condition is false.
An else clause holds statements that run when the if condition is false.
and returns True only if both conditions are true; or returns True if either is true; not inverts a single condition.

anchors.quote: When an if-else statement is executed, one and only one of the branches is taken
If the condition is true, the body is executed. If the condition is false, the body is not executed
An else statement is used with an if statement and contains a body of statements that is executed when the if statement's condition is false
The and operator takes two condition operands and returns True if both conditions are true

attribution: OpenStax Introduction to Python Programming, §4.2 If-else statements; §4.3 Boolean operations

facts: A conditional statement chooses which block of code to run based on whether a condition is true; if-else takes exactly one branch, and boolean operators (and, or, not) build compound conditions.
An if statement runs its body only when the condition is true, and skips it when the condition is false.
An else clause holds statements that run when the if condition is false.
and returns True only if both conditions are true; or returns True if either is true; not inverts a single condition.

keyTerms.df: A conditional statement selects a block according to whether its condition is true.
keyTerms.eg: When a condition is true, the conditional statement chooses which block runs.
keyTerms.mi: A conditional statement requires boolean operators to choose a block.
keyTerms.cx: Block selection can be based on whether a condition is true; a compound condition is not required.

keyTerms.df: An if statement is a conditional form whose body runs when its condition is true.
keyTerms.eg: When the if condition is false, the if statement skips its body.
keyTerms.mi: An if statement runs its body when its condition is false.
keyTerms.cx: A false condition leads the body to be skipped, not run.

keyTerms.df: An else clause contains statements associated with a false if condition.
keyTerms.eg: If the condition is false, the statements in the else clause run.
keyTerms.mi: An else clause holds statements for a true if condition.
keyTerms.cx: Its statements correspond to the condition being false rather than true.

scenario.su: A student must label which block runs in an if-else before a deadline, with the recorded if condition marked false. The student must also distinguish a compound condition recorded as true or false, using the noted and, or, and not operators.
scenario.ma: if condition notation marked false, if-body observation marked skipped, else-clause observation marked run, and-or-not condition table marked true or false

mc.q: An if statement condition is observed as false beside an else clause containing statements. Which comparison correctly distinguishes what happens to the if statement and else clause?
op: The if body skips; else statements run
The if body runs; else statements skip
Both if and else statements run
Both if and else statements skip
mc.ex: A false condition makes the if statement skip its body and makes the else clause statements run. The if body does not run while the else statements skip.

mc.q: A compound condition records one condition as true and the other as false; students must classify both results before a deadline. Which notation correctly compares and with or?
op: and is False; or is True
and is True; or is False
and and or are both True
and and or are both False
mc.ex: and returns True only when both conditions are true, while or returns True when either condition is true. They therefore do not both return True for these recorded conditions.

facts: A conditional statement chooses which block of code to run based on whether a condition is true; if-else takes exactly one branch, and boolean operators (and, or, not) build compound conditions.
An if statement runs its body only when the condition is true, and skips it when the condition is false.
An else clause holds statements that run when the if condition is false.
and returns True only if both conditions are true; or returns True if either is true; not inverts a single condition.

keyTerms.df: A conditional statement selects which code block executes based on a condition's truth value.
keyTerms.eg: An if statement runs its body only when the condition is true.
keyTerms.mi: A conditional statement executes multiple code blocks depending on the condition's truth value.
keyTerms.cx: A conditional statement takes exactly one branch, meaning it chooses only one path based on the condition's truth value.

keyTerms.df: An if statement executes its body only when the specified condition evaluates to true.
keyTerms.eg: An if statement runs its body only when the condition is true.
keyTerms.mi: An if statement executes its body when the condition is false and skips it when true.
keyTerms.cx: An if statement skips its body when the condition is false, executing it only when the condition is true.

keyTerms.df: Boolean operators are used to construct compound conditions using and, or, and not.
keyTerms.eg: Boolean operators (and, or, not) build compound conditions.
keyTerms.mi: Boolean operators only invert a single condition to determine the final outcome.
keyTerms.cx: Boolean operators not inverts a single condition; they build compound conditions using and, or, not.

scenario.su: A program checks if a user's age is over eighteen to grant access to a restricted area. The program must handle the case where the age is below the threshold by displaying an error message instead.
scenario.ma: Compare the logic for checking age 17 and age 20 against the requirement that an if statement runs its body only when the condition is true.

mc.q: Distinguish between the behavior of an if statement and an else clause regarding code execution flow.
op: The if statement runs its body when the condition is false.
The else clause runs its body when the condition is true.
The if statement skips its body when the condition is false.
The else clause runs its body when the condition is false.
mc.ex: An if statement skips its body when the condition is false, while the else clause holds statements that run when the if condition is false.

mc.q: Determine the result of a compound condition using boolean operators when checking if a user is an administrator or a moderator.
op: The condition returns True if both parts are false.
The condition returns True if either part is true.
The condition returns True only if both parts are true.
The condition returns True if the 'not' operator is used.
mc.ex: The condition returns True if either part is true, which is the behavior of the or operator.

lessonInput.title: Integumentary system and skin layers
lessonInput.objectives: Use only the supplied claims to make a defensible distinction without adding outside facts.
lessonInput.topics: Claim 0: The integumentary system includes the skin and accessory structures; skin has epidermal and dermal layers that support protection and communication. Claim 1: The skin has two main layers: the epidermis and dermis. Claim 2: The epidermis is made of keratinized stratified squamous epithelium.

claims: The integumentary system includes the skin and accessory structures; skin has epidermal and dermal layers that support protection and communication.
The skin has two main layers: the epidermis and dermis.
The epidermis is made of keratinized stratified squamous epithelium.

anchors.quote: The skin and its accessory structures make up the integumentary system
The skin is composed of two main layers: the epidermis
The epidermis is composed of keratinized, stratified squamous epithelium

facts: The integumentary system includes the skin and accessory structures; skin has epidermal and dermal layers that support protection and communication.
The skin has two main layers: the epidermis and dermis.
The epidermis is made of keratinized stratified squamous epithelium.

keyTerms.df: Skin belongs to the integumentary system and has epidermal and dermal layers.
keyTerms.eg: A system notation lists skin alongside accessory structures.
keyTerms.mi: Skin is made of keratinized stratified squamous epithelium.
keyTerms.cx: That tissue description applies to the epidermis; skin has epidermal and dermal layers.

keyTerms.df: The epidermis is a main skin layer made of keratinized stratified squamous epithelium.
keyTerms.eg: A layer notation pairs the epidermis with the dermis.
keyTerms.mi: The epidermis includes the skin and accessory structures.
keyTerms.cx: Those structures belong within the integumentary system; the epidermis is a skin layer.

keyTerms.df: The dermis is one of the skin's two main layers, paired with the epidermis.
keyTerms.eg: A skin record names epidermal and dermal layers supporting protection and communication.
keyTerms.mi: The dermis is made of keratinized stratified squamous epithelium.
keyTerms.cx: Keratinized stratified squamous epithelium describes the epidermis; the dermis is a main skin layer.

scenario.su: A student editor must assign subject labels to three anatomy notations before a deadline. One notation lists skin and accessory structures, another lists epidermal and dermal layers, and a third names keratinized stratified squamous epithelium, so each label must match the stated subject.
scenario.ma: system passage listing skin and accessory structures, layer notation naming the epidermis and dermis, tissue observation naming keratinized stratified squamous epithelium

mc.q: A comparison records that the integumentary system includes skin and accessory structures, while skin has epidermal and dermal layers. Which proposition preserves the distinction between integumentary system and skin?
op: Accessory structures have epidermal and dermal layers.
Epidermis includes skin and accessory structures.
Dermis includes skin and accessory structures.
Skin has epidermal and dermal layers.
mc.ex: The skin is stated to have epidermal and dermal layers within the integumentary system. Accessory structures are included in the system, but the layer relation is stated for skin.

mc.q: An anatomy notation identifies keratinized stratified squamous epithelium, and the editor must attach the correct subject label before the deadline. Which label-and-description proposition matches the recorded tissue observation?
op: Integumentary system is keratinized stratified squamous epithelium.
Dermis is keratinized stratified squamous epithelium.
Skin is keratinized stratified squamous epithelium.
Epidermis is keratinized stratified squamous epithelium.
mc.ex: The epidermis is stated to be made of keratinized stratified squamous epithelium. The dermis is a main skin layer, but the tissue description is assigned to the epidermis.

facts: The integumentary system includes the skin and accessory structures; skin has epidermal and dermal layers that support protection and communication.
The skin has two main layers: the epidermis and dermis.
The epidermis is made of keratinized stratified squamous epithelium.

keyTerms.df: The integumentary system encompasses the skin and its accessory structures which function to provide protection and communication.
keyTerms.eg: The skin and its accessory structures provide protection and communication.
keyTerms.mi: The integumentary system is only the skin and does not include accessory structures.
keyTerms.cx: The integumentary system includes the skin and accessory structures which function to provide protection and communication.

keyTerms.df: The epidermis is a layer of the skin composed of keratinized stratified squamous epithelium that provides primary protection.
keyTerms.eg: The epidermis is made of keratinized stratified squamous epithelium.
keyTerms.mi: The epidermis is a simple layer of skin that lacks keratinization.
keyTerms.cx: The epidermis is made of keratinized stratified squamous epithelium, which is a specific structural composition.

keyTerms.df: The dermis is one of the two main layers of the skin that supports the epidermis and facilitates communication.
keyTerms.eg: The skin has two main layers: the epidermis and dermis.
keyTerms.mi: The dermis is the outermost layer of the skin that is primarily responsible for keratinization.
keyTerms.cx: The dermis is one of the two main layers of the skin that supports the epidermis and facilitates communication.

scenario.su: A patient presents with a deep abrasion on their forearm, and a nurse observes the skin surface exhibiting a thick, tough outer layer. The nurse must determine which layer is responsible for this specific protective feature.
scenario.ma: The nurse compares the observation of the thick, tough outer layer to the description of the epidermis, and notes the presence of the dermal layer beneath it.

mc.q: When examining a deep abrasion, which layer is primarily responsible for the thick, tough outer layer of the skin structure?
op: The dermis provides the thick, tough outer layer.
The epidermis provides the thick, tough outer layer.
The epidermis supports communication and protection.
The dermis is made of keratinized stratified epithelium.
mc.ex: The epidermis is made of keratinized stratified squamous epithelium, which is the subject evidence supporting the answer, then correct the closest distractor.

mc.q: A student is studying the skin layers and observes that the skin has two main layers, one of which is the epidermis, while another layer supports communication.
op: The dermis is made of keratinized stratified squamous epithelium.
The epidermis supports communication and protection.
The dermis is the outermost layer of the skin.
The epidermis is the layer that supports communication.
mc.ex: The skin has two main layers: the epidermis and dermis, which is the subject evidence supporting the answer, then correct the closest distractor.

lessonInput.title: File input and output
lessonInput.objectives: Use only the supplied claims to make a defensible distinction without adding outside facts.
lessonInput.topics: Claim 0: File I/O lets a program read information from and write information into files; a file is accessed by opening it, working with its contents, and closing it. Claim 1: open() returns a file object that the program then reads from or writes to. Claim 2: read() reads the entire contents of a file and returns a single string. Claim 3: readline() returns the next single line, while readlines() returns a list with every line of the file.
lessonInput.readings: OpenStax Introduction to Python Programming, §14.1 Reading from files

claims: File I/O lets a program read information from and write information into files; a file is accessed by opening it, working with its contents, and closing it.
open() returns a file object that the program then reads from or writes to.
read() reads the entire contents of a file and returns a single string.
readline() returns the next single line, while readlines() returns a list with every line of the file.

anchors.quote: Python supports the opening of a file using the open() function
Python supports the opening of a file using the open() function
The read() function reads the contents of a file and returns a string
The readlines() function reads the individual lines of a file and returns a string list containing all the lines of the file in order

attribution: OpenStax Introduction to Python Programming, §14.1 Reading from files

facts: File I/O lets a program read information from and write information into files; a file is accessed by opening it, working with its contents, and closing it.
open() returns a file object that the program then reads from or writes to.
read() reads the entire contents of a file and returns a single string.
readline() returns the next single line, while readlines() returns a list with every line of the file.

keyTerms.df: A file object is what open() returns for a program to read from or write to.
keyTerms.eg: The program receives a file object from open().
keyTerms.mi: A file object is the single string returned by read().
keyTerms.cx: The object comes from open(); read() instead produces a string containing the entire contents.

keyTerms.df: read() is a file operation that returns the entire contents as one string.
keyTerms.eg: A program applies read() and receives the entire contents in a single string.
keyTerms.mi: read() returns the next single line from the file.
keyTerms.cx: The next-line result belongs to readline(), whereas read() produces the entire contents.

keyTerms.df: readlines() is a file operation whose returned value is a list containing every line.
keyTerms.eg: A program applies readlines() and receives a list with every line of the file.
keyTerms.mi: readlines() returns the entire contents as a single string.
keyTerms.cx: The every-line result from readlines() is a list; the single-string result comes from read().

scenario.su: A program review must classify two recorded file results before a deadline. The reviewer must distinguish a single string containing the entire contents from the next single line.
scenario.ma: read() result notation: entire contents returned as a single string, readline() result notation: next single line returned

mc.q: A review compares read() returning the entire contents as one string with readline() returning the next line. Which statement preserves the observed distinction?
op: read() returns one string; readline() returns next line
Both return the next single line
read() returns next line; readline() returns one string
Both return entire contents as one string
mc.ex: read() returns the entire contents as a single string, while readline() returns the next single line. They do not exchange those results.

mc.q: A review records that a call returned a list with every line of the file, and the label must be chosen before a deadline. Which label matches the observation?
op: The call was readline()
The call was read()
The call was open()
The call was readlines()
mc.ex: A list containing every line is the result specified for readlines(). readline() instead produces the next single line.

facts: File I/O lets a program read information from and write information into files; a file is accessed by opening it, working with its contents, and closing it.
open() returns a file object that the program then reads from or writes to.
read() reads the entire contents of a file and returns a single string.
readline() returns the next single line, while readlines() returns a list with every line of the file.

keyTerms.df: File I/O is the process that allows a program to read information from and write information into files.
keyTerms.eg: A program uses File I/O to save user data to a text file and later retrieve that data.
keyTerms.mi: File I/O is simply the act of typing data directly into a file without using a program.
keyTerms.cx: File I/O is the mechanism that enables a program to read and write information into files.

keyTerms.df: The open() function returns a file object that the program subsequently uses to read from or write to.
keyTerms.eg: Calling open() creates a file object that allows subsequent read() or write() operations on the file.
keyTerms.mi: open() is a command that directly writes data into the file without creating a file object for later use.
keyTerms.cx: open() is the function that generates a file object for subsequent reading or writing operations.

keyTerms.df: The read() function reads the entire contents of a file and returns that content as a single string.
keyTerms.eg: Using read() on a file retrieves all the text within that file as one continuous string.
keyTerms.mi: read() only reads the first line of a file and returns that line as a string.
keyTerms.cx: read() reads the entire contents of a file and returns a single string, not just the first line.

scenario.su: A data processing script needs to read configuration settings from a text file and then update a specific setting within that file. The constraint is that the script must handle the file access safely by ensuring the file is properly closed after all operations are complete.
scenario.ma: Compare the behavior of read() and readline() when processing a configuration file containing three distinct lines of settings.

mc.q: When a program uses read() on a file, what is the resulting data structure returned to the program?
op: A single string containing all file contents
A list of lines from the file
A file object for further operations
A dictionary mapping keys to values
mc.ex: read() reads the entire contents of a file and returns a single string, then correct the closest distractor.

mc.q: A developer is writing code to process a log file where each entry is on a new line, and they need to iterate through every entry sequentially. Which method should they use?
op: A() to get the file object
read() to get the whole file content
readline() to get the next single line
readlines() to get a list of every line
mc.ex: readline() returns the next single line, while readlines() returns a list with every line of the file, then correct the closest distractor.

lessonInput.title: Process and progress indicators
lessonInput.objectives: Use only the supplied claims to make a defensible distinction without adding outside facts.
lessonInput.topics: Claim 0: Process lists explain sequential instructions, while step indicators show a user’s current position in a linear multi-page flow. Claim 1: A step indicator suits a linear process with at least three high-level steps across multiple screens. Claim 2: The indicator complements back and next controls; it is not navigation by itself. Claim 3: Completion and current-step meaning must not rely on color alone. Claim 4: The current labeled step should be exposed programmatically with aria-current.
lessonInput.readings: U.S. Web Design System, U.S. General Services Administration

claims: Process lists explain sequential instructions, while step indicators show a user’s current position in a linear multi-page flow.
A step indicator suits a linear process with at least three high-level steps across multiple screens.
The indicator complements back and next controls; it is not navigation by itself.
Completion and current-step meaning must not rely on color alone.
The current labeled step should be exposed programmatically with aria-current.

anchors.quote: updates users on their progress
three or more high-level steps
not to be navigation of its own
make the completion status of each step explicit
use aria-current="true"

attribution: U.S. Web Design System, U.S. General Services Administration

facts: Process lists explain sequential instructions, while step indicators show a user’s current position in a linear multi-page flow.
A step indicator suits a linear process with at least three high-level steps across multiple screens.
The indicator complements back and next controls; it is not navigation by itself.
Completion and current-step meaning must not rely on color alone.
The current labeled step should be exposed programmatically with aria-current.

keyTerms.df: Process lists are instructions arranged as a sequence.
keyTerms.eg: The U.S. Web Design System uses a process list to explain sequential instructions.
keyTerms.mi: Process lists show a user’s current position across multiple screens.
keyTerms.cx: Showing current position in a linear multi-page flow is the role of step indicators.

keyTerms.df: A step indicator marks current position within a linear process spanning multiple screens.
keyTerms.eg: A step indicator shows the current labeled step alongside back and next controls.
keyTerms.mi: A step indicator replaces back and next controls as navigation.
keyTerms.cx: Users still need back and next controls because the indicator merely complements them.

keyTerms.df: Aria-current programmatically exposes which labeled step is current.
keyTerms.eg: The current labeled step in the U.S. Web Design System is exposed with aria-current.
keyTerms.mi: Aria-current makes color sufficient for communicating completion and current-step meaning.
keyTerms.cx: Completion and current-step meaning require more than color, regardless of programmatic exposure.

scenario.su: A U.S. Web Design System review covers a linear process with three high-level steps across multiple screens, but its indicator is expected to replace back and next controls. Students must classify that expectation while checking a current labeled step shown by color under a deadline.
scenario.ma: three-step multi-screen flow design, back-and-next control design, color-based current-step observation, aria-current notation

mc.q: A review compares process lists that present sequential instructions with step indicators that display current position across multiple screens; which distinction matches the observed designs?
op: Both designs show current position
Process lists show position; step indicators instruct
Both designs explain sequential instructions
Process lists instruct; step indicators show position
mc.ex: Process lists explain sequential instructions, whereas step indicators show current position in a linear multi-page flow. Treating the two designs as interchangeable reverses their stated roles.

mc.q: A linear process has three high-level steps across multiple screens, and its indicator appears beside back and next controls; how should reviewers classify the indicator?
op: Suitable navigation replacing back and next controls
Process list complementing back and next controls
Suitable indicator complementing back and next controls
Process list replacing back and next controls
mc.ex: Three high-level steps across multiple screens make a step indicator suitable, and the indicator complements back and next controls. It does not replace those controls as navigation.

facts: Process lists explain sequential instructions, while step indicators show a user’s current position in a linear multi-page flow.
A step indicator suits a linear process with at least three high-level steps across multiple screens.
The indicator complements back and next controls; it is not navigation by itself.
Completion and current-step meaning must not rely on color alone.
The current labeled step should be exposed programmatically with aria-current.

keyTerms.df: Process lists explain sequential instructions for a task.
keyTerms.eg: A process list detailing the steps required to complete a multi-page form.
keyTerms.mi: Process lists are only for showing the order of steps in a flow.
keyTerms.cx: Process lists explain sequential instructions, while step indicators show a user’s current position in a linear multi-page flow.

keyTerms.df: Step indicators show a user’s current position within a linear multi-page flow.
keyTerms.eg: A step indicator showing the user is on step two of a four-step checkout process.
keyTerms.mi: Step indicators are used exclusively for showing the final completion status of a task.
keyTerms.cx: Step indicators show a user’s current position in a linear multi-page flow, and they complement back and next controls.

keyTerms.df: The current labeled step should be exposed programmatically with aria-current.
keyTerms.eg: Using aria-current to programmatically mark the active step in a multi-page flow.
keyTerms.mi: aria-current is a visual styling method used to highlight the current step.
keyTerms.cx: The current labeled step should be exposed programmatically with aria-current, not relying on visual styling.

scenario.su: A user is navigating a multi-page service application that requires completing at least three high-level steps across different screens. The user needs a clear way to understand their progress without relying solely on visual cues. The constraint is that the indicator must not rely on color alone to convey meaning.
scenario.ma: Compare the process list showing sequential instructions with the step indicator showing the user's current position in a linear multi-page flow.

mc.q: When designing a linear multi-page flow, what is the primary function of a step indicator in relation to process lists?
op: Step indicators are used for showing the final completion status of a task.
Step indicators show a user’s current position in a linear multi-page flow.
Step indicators are only for showing the order of steps in a flow.
Step indicators are used exclusively for showing sequential instructions.
mc.ex: Process lists explain sequential instructions, while step indicators show a user’s current position in a linear multi-page flow, then step indicators show a user’s current position in a linear multi-page flow.

mc.q: A designer is choosing between a process list and a step indicator for a linear process that spans multiple screens; what is the correct choice?
op: A process list is the only way to show the user's current position.
A step indicator suits a linear process with at least three high-level steps across multiple screens.
A process list is better when the flow has fewer than three high-level steps.
A step indicator is not navigation by itself but complements back and next controls.
mc.ex: A step indicator suits a linear process with at least three high-level steps across multiple screens, then a step indicator suits a linear process with at least three high-level steps across multiple screens.

lessonInput.title: DC circuits
lessonInput.objectives: Use only the supplied claims to make a defensible distinction without adding outside facts.
lessonInput.topics: Claim 0: A DC circuit is a conducting path with steady current, sources, and components whose voltages and currents obey conservation rules. Claim 1: Series components share the same current; parallel branches share the same voltage. Claim 2: Kirchhoff's junction rule expresses charge conservation, and the loop rule expresses energy conservation.

claims: A DC circuit is a conducting path with steady current, sources, and components whose voltages and currents obey conservation rules.
Series components share the same current; parallel branches share the same voltage.
Kirchhoff's junction rule expresses charge conservation, and the loop rule expresses energy conservation.

anchors.quote: direct-current circuits
series and parallel resistors
Kirchhoff's rules

facts: A DC circuit is a conducting path with steady current, sources, and components whose voltages and currents obey conservation rules.
Series components share the same current; parallel branches share the same voltage.
Kirchhoff's junction rule expresses charge conservation, and the loop rule expresses energy conservation.

keyTerms.df: A DC circuit is a conducting path distinguished by steady current, sources, components, and conservation rules.
keyTerms.eg: A conducting path with steady current, sources, and components is a DC circuit.
keyTerms.mi: A DC circuit has component voltages and currents that oppose conservation rules.
keyTerms.cx: Its component voltages and currents obey conservation rules along the conducting path.

keyTerms.df: Series components are circuit components distinguished by sharing the same current.
keyTerms.eg: Two series components in a DC circuit carry the same current.
keyTerms.mi: Series components are identified by sharing the same voltage.
keyTerms.cx: Shared current characterizes series components, while shared voltage characterizes parallel branches.

keyTerms.df: The junction rule is a Kirchhoff rule that expresses charge conservation.
keyTerms.eg: Kirchhoff's junction rule and loop rule express charge and energy conservation, respectively.
keyTerms.mi: The junction rule expresses energy conservation rather than charge conservation.
keyTerms.cx: Charge conservation corresponds to the junction rule; energy conservation corresponds to the loop rule.

scenario.su: Students must label a conducting path as a DC circuit and distinguish its series components from its parallel branches before a deadline. The steady-current notation, component current comparison, and branch voltage comparison must support one defensible classification despite the time constraint.
scenario.ma: steady-current path diagram, component current comparison, branch voltage comparison

mc.q: A circuit notation shows equal current through series components and equal voltage across parallel branches; which comparison correctly distinguishes the two observed component relations?
op: Series share current; parallel branches share voltage
Series share voltage; parallel branches share current
Series and parallel branches share current
Series and parallel components share voltage
mc.ex: Series components share the same current, whereas parallel branches share the same voltage. The reversed comparison incorrectly exchanges these two relations.

mc.q: A student compares junction notation tied to charge conservation with loop notation tied to energy conservation; which labels fit the records before the workshop deadline?
op: Junction: charge conservation; loop: energy conservation
Junction: energy conservation; loop: charge conservation
Junction and loop: charge conservation
Junction and loop: energy conservation
mc.ex: The junction rule expresses charge conservation, and the loop rule expresses energy conservation. Assigning energy to the junction and charge to the loop reverses the supported labels.

facts: A DC circuit is a conducting path with steady current, sources, and components whose voltages and currents obey conservation rules.
Series components share the same current; parallel branches share the same voltage.
Kirchhoff's junction rule expresses charge conservation, and the loop rule expresses energy conservation.

keyTerms.df: A conducting path with steady current, sources, and components whose voltages and currents obey conservation rules.
keyTerms.eg: A circuit where a battery and a resistor are connected in a single path.
keyTerms.mi: A DC circuit only involves components that have constant voltage and current.
keyTerms.cx: A DC circuit involves sources and components whose voltages and currents obey conservation rules.

keyTerms.df: Components connected in series share the same current flowing through them.
keyTerms.eg: Two resistors connected end-to-end in a single wire.
keyTerms.mi: In series circuits, the voltage across each component is identical.
keyTerms.cx: In series circuits, the current is the same, but the voltage across each component is not necessarily identical.

keyTerms.df: Branches connected in parallel share the same voltage across them.
keyTerms.eg: Two light bulbs connected across the same power source.

keyTerms.cx: Parallel branches require the voltage across every branch to be the same, not the current.

mc.q: When analyzing a DC circuit, which rule is used to express energy conservation across a closed path?
op: The junction rule expresses energy conservation
The loop rule expresses energy conservation
The series rule expresses energy conservation
The parallel rule expresses energy conservation
mc.ex: The loop rule expresses energy conservation, then the junction rule expresses charge conservation, then the series rule expresses current sharing.

op: Branches must share the same current
Branches must share the same voltage

lessonInput.title: Journey mapping
lessonInput.objectives: Use only the supplied claims to make a defensible distinction without adding outside facts.
lessonInput.topics: Claim 0: Journey mapping represents an end-to-end experience from the user's perspective so a team can see connected steps, boundaries, breakdowns, and opportunities. Claim 1: A journey map should start from research about the steps users actually take and the transactions involved. Claim 2: An experience map should make struggle points and candidate improvement areas visible. Claim 3: A map can reveal dead ends where the user cannot continue toward the larger goal. Claim 4: Journey analysis should include gaps between online and offline parts of a service.

claims: Journey mapping represents an end-to-end experience from the user's perspective so a team can see connected steps, boundaries, breakdowns, and opportunities.
A journey map should start from research about the steps users actually take and the transactions involved.
An experience map should make struggle points and candidate improvement areas visible.
A map can reveal dead ends where the user cannot continue toward the larger goal.
Journey analysis should include gaps between online and offline parts of a service.

anchors.quote: It's important for teams to make sure the thing they're building forms a coherent part of a user's wider journey.
Start by talking to your users to learn more about the steps they have to take and the transactions involved.
The map should show which bits of the journey users are struggling with and the areas you might want to focus on improving.
dead ends in the user journey
online and offline elements of the transaction not joining up in an intuitive way

keyTerms.df: Journey mapping represents an end-to-end experience from the user's perspective.
keyTerms.eg: Journey mapping shows connected steps, boundaries, breakdowns, and opportunities.
keyTerms.mi: Journey mapping represents separate transactions rather than an end-to-end experience.
keyTerms.cx: It connects the experience from the user's perspective across its steps and boundaries.

keyTerms.df: An experience map makes struggle points and candidate improvement areas visible.
keyTerms.eg: An experience map shows a struggle point beside a candidate improvement area.
keyTerms.mi: An experience map makes transactions involved visible instead of struggle points.
keyTerms.cx: Its visible subjects are struggle points and candidate improvement areas.

keyTerms.df: Dead ends are points where the user cannot continue toward the larger goal.
keyTerms.eg: A map shows a dead end between connected steps toward the larger goal.
keyTerms.mi: Dead ends are gaps between online and offline parts of a service.
keyTerms.cx: They mark where continuation toward the larger goal is not possible.

scenario.su: A team must classify what its map shows before a deadline: connected steps and boundaries across an end-to-end experience, plus struggle points and candidate improvement areas. The team must distinguish the map's two supported roles while also checking a recorded gap between online and offline parts of the service.
scenario.ma: research record of steps users actually take and transactions involved, notation of connected steps and boundaries, observation of struggle points and candidate improvement areas, notation of the online-offline gap

mc.q: A team compares connected steps and boundaries across an end-to-end experience with visible struggle points and candidate improvement areas. Which distinction between journey mapping and an experience map is supported?
op: Journey mapping exposes struggles; experience maps connect
Both represent connected steps and boundaries
Both show struggle points and improvement areas
Journey mapping connects; experience maps expose struggles
mc.ex: Journey mapping represents the end-to-end experience and connected elements, while an experience map makes struggles and improvement areas visible. Assigning those roles in reverse swaps the supplied relations.

mc.q: Research records the steps users actually take and their transactions, while a notation shows the user cannot continue toward the larger goal. Under a deadline, what should the team identify?
op: Dead ends ground research into user transactions
Research grounds visible candidate improvement areas
Research grounds a journey map revealing dead ends
Transactions reveal online and offline gaps
mc.ex: The recorded steps and transactions provide the research basis for a journey map, and the blocked continuation is a dead end the map can reveal. Candidate improvement areas belong to what an experience map makes visible.

facts: Journey mapping represents an end-to-end experience from the user's perspective so a team can see connected steps, boundaries, breakdowns, and opportunities.
A journey map should start from research about the steps users actually take and the transactions involved.
An experience map should make struggle points and candidate improvement areas visible.
A map can reveal dead ends where the user cannot continue toward the larger goal.

keyTerms.df: Journey mapping is an end-to-end experience from the user's perspective allowing a team to see connected steps, boundaries, breakdowns, and opportunities.
keyTerms.eg: A team uses a journey map to visualize the entire process a user goes through from start to finish.
keyTerms.mi: Journey mapping is just a simple list of steps a user takes without considering the emotional or contextual experience.
keyTerms.cx: Journey mapping requires seeing connected steps, boundaries, breakdowns, and opportunities from the user's perspective.

keyTerms.df: An experience map is a tool designed to make struggle points and candidate improvement areas visible within a service.
keyTerms.eg: An experience map highlights where users encounter friction or where improvements are needed in the service flow.
keyTerms.mi: An experience map is identical to a journey map but focuses only on the positive aspects of the user's interaction.
keyTerms.cx: An experience map specifically makes struggle points and candidate improvement areas visible, unlike a simple list.

keyTerms.df: Journey analysis involves examining gaps between online and offline parts of a service to identify areas for improvement.
keyTerms.eg: Journey analysis looks at the disconnect between a website process and the physical steps a user takes in a store.
keyTerms.mi: Journey analysis is only about looking at the online steps and ignoring any offline interactions or physical environments.
keyTerms.cx: Journey analysis must include gaps between online and offline parts of a service to be comprehensive.

scenario.su: A team is mapping the process for a customer to return a faulty product online. The actionable problem is identifying where the user encounters a dead end in the return process. The constraint is that the team only has access to the online transaction steps and cannot observe the physical return location.
scenario.ma: Compare the map showing the online return steps with the map showing the physical return steps.

mc.q: Which concept distinguishes a journey map from an experience map based on what they reveal about the user's path?
op: Journey mapping shows connected steps and boundaries.
Experience map shows struggle points and improvement areas.
Journey mapping reveals dead ends where users cannot continue.
Experience map includes gaps between online and offline parts.
mc.ex: Journey mapping represents an end-to-end experience from the user's perspective so a team can see connected steps, boundaries, breakdowns, and opportunities. An experience map should make struggle points and candidate improvement areas visible.

mc.q: When analyzing a service, what specific element must journey analysis include to provide a complete view of the user's interaction?
op: Identifying dead ends where the user cannot continue toward the larger goal.
Researching the steps users actually take and the transactions involved.
Making struggle points and candidate improvement areas visible.
Including gaps between online and offline parts of a service.
mc.ex: Journey analysis should include gaps between online and offline parts of a service. A journey map should start from research about the steps users actually take and the transactions involved.
